nameStory: The Long-tubercled Spikerush gets its name from two key features that help identify it. The "spike" refers to its distinctive flower cluster that looks like a tiny, dense spike at the tip of each stem. The "long-tubercled" part comes from the swollen base of the flower's style (called a tubercle) that's noticeably larger than most of its spikerush cousins - up to 2.5mm across!
description: Long-tubercled Spikerush is a wetland perennial that forms dense, grass-like clumps in soggy soils. It sends up slender, leafless stems that can reach over 2 feet tall, each topped with a small, oval-shaped flower spike. Unlike true grasses, these stems are distinctly elliptical when you roll them between your fingers rather than round or flat. The plant spreads by underground runners to create thick colonies that help stabilize muddy shorelines and wet meadows.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, dense oval spikes sit at the tip of each stem like tiny brown footballs, with the distinctive large white to pale orange-brown tubercle (swollen style base) often spotted with red - this is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps of numerous upright stems that emerge directly from the ground with no visible leaves, creating a pin-cushion appearance in wet areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, leafless stems up to 70cm tall that feel distinctly elliptical (oval-shaped) when rolled between your thumb and finger, not round like many rushes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Essentially leafless above ground - what look like stems are actually the plant's photosynthetic parts, with only small scale-like structures at the base

habitat: Look for Long-tubercled Spikerush in consistently wet or seasonally flooded areas throughout New England's coastal regions and inland wetlands. It thrives in the muddy edges of ponds, slow streams, marshes, and wet meadows where the soil stays soggy most of the year. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland sedges, rushes, and cattails in areas that may be underwater in spring but just muddy by late summer.

seasonality.spring: New stems emerge from underground rhizomes as waters recede, forming fresh green clumps. Early flower spikes begin developing at stem tips by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs with prominent spikes displaying the characteristic large tubercles. This is the best time for identification when the diagnostic swollen style bases are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Stems begin to turn brown and seeds mature and disperse. The distinctive tubercles may still be visible on dried flower heads.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, leaving only dried stem bases. The plant survives underground via rhizomes until spring emergence.

funFact: Despite being recorded in New England only twice according to recent observations, this spikerush is actually found along the entire Atlantic and Gulf coasts - it's like finding a rare coastal treasure that somehow made its way to our northern wetlands!
confusionNotes: Long-tubercled Spikerush can easily be confused with its many spikerush relatives, but the large tubercle (up to 2.5mm) is your best clue - most other spikerushes have much smaller or differently shaped tubercles. Remember: "Long-tubercled = Large tubercle" to distinguish it from common spikerush and other relatives with smaller swollen style bases.
contextualKnowledge: Spikerushes belong to the sedge family, not the grass family, despite their grass-like appearance. The old botanist's rhyme "sedges have edges" applies here - though spikerush stems are more elliptical than sharply three-angled like many sedges, they're still not perfectly round like true grasses.
compareHints: Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.5mm across compared to the much smaller tubercles of Common Spikerush or Needle Spikerush. While Blunt Spikerush may be similar in size, its tubercle is distinctly smaller and differently shaped. The elliptical stem cross-section also helps separate it from the more angular stems of some relatives like Squarestem Spikerush.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
